The Spanish flag snapper (Lutjanus carponotatus) from the Great Barrier Reef exhibits distinct life-history parameters that reflect its position as a medium-bodied lutjanid. Females reach a maximum fork length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a value derived from extensive tag-recapture data across multiple reef systems over a decade. In contrast, males achieve a smaller asymptotic size, attaining a maximum fork length of 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters], a pattern common among protogynous or size-dimorphic serranids and lutjanids. These ultimate lengths are among the smaller recorded for the genus Lutjanus, with larger congeners like the mangrove red snapper exceeding 60 centimeters. The asymptotic mass for females, calculated from length-weight relationships fitted to a large sample of mature individuals, is approximately 859 grams [Wwi = approximately 859 grams], reflecting the slightly compressed, deep-bodied morphology typical of reef-associated snappers. This adult body mass represents a considerable investment in somatic tissue before the onset of reproductive activity, which in this species is delayed relative to many smaller-bodied tropical reef fishes.

Reproductive development in female Spanish flag snapper is characterized by a relatively early onset of gonadal maturation. Field studies based on histological examination of ovarian tissue indicate that females reach puberty at a fork length of 18.6 centimeters [Lp = 18.6 centimeters], a size that corresponds to approximately the second year of life under the thermal conditions typical of inshore reef habitats at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This length at maturity is relatively small compared to the ultimate size, suggesting that females allocate resources to reproduction well before reaching their full somatic potential, a strategy that buffers against unpredictable recruitment success in the variable reef environment. The size at first reproduction is consistent with values reported for other tropical lutjanids of similar body plan, such as Lutjanus argentimaculatus, though slightly lower than that observed in populations from higher-latitude reefs where cooler temperatures slow growth and delay maturation.

Neonatal body mass in Lutjanus carponotatus is remarkably low, reflecting the species' pelagic egg and larval strategy. Based on an average egg diameter of 0.85 millimeters observed in the congener Lutjanus stellatus, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams] for newly hatched yolk-sac larvae. This minute initial mass, characteristic of broadcast-spawning teleosts, means that larvae emerge with only a small endowment of yolk reserves and must rapidly commence exogenous feeding within a few days of hatching. The transition from lecithotrophic to exotrophic feeding represents a critical bottleneck; larvae that fail to locate suitable planktonic prey by the time of yolk-sac resorption suffer irreversible starvation. Field collections of ichthyoplankton across the central Great Barrier Reef indicate that newly hatched prolarvae of this species are among the smallest lutjanid larvae in the region, potentially influencing their dispersal potential and vulnerability to predation.

Under controlled laboratory conditions designed to simulate summer spawning temperatures at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum reproductive output of female Spanish flag snapper has been characterized through a combination of batch fecundity estimates and spawning frequency observations. Females produce approximately 749,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 749,000 eggs per spawning event], a single clutch that reflects the large gonad volume relative to body size in this species. The frequency of spawning during the peak reproductive season is estimated at one spawning event every 365 days [F_R_i = one spawning event every 365 days], indicating that this species is a single-batch spawner that releases its entire annual fecundity in one synchronized event each year. This iteroparous strategy, combined with high batch fecundity but low spawning frequency, contrasts with the multiple-batch spawning observed in many smaller lutjanids and may reflect a trade-off between egg size, larval survival, and the energetic costs of repeated gonad recrudescence.

Longevity in Lutjanus carponotatus is moderate for a reef-associated lutjanid, with the oldest individuals recorded in the wild reaching a lifespan of 20 years [am = 20 years] under the ambient thermal regime of the Great Barrier Reef at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This estimate, derived from otolith increment analysis of a large sample of adult fish, positions the species between short-lived tropical gobies and long-lived deep-water eteline snappers such as Etelis coruscans, which can exceed 40 years. The age structure of the population suggests that natural mortality is relatively low for adults, allowing individuals to accumulate multiple reproductive events across their lifespan. Annual mortality estimates from catch curve analysis indicate that once individuals reach 36 centimeters in fork length, survival rates remain high, with only a gradual decline in condition associated with reproductive senescence in the oldest age classes, typically those beyond 15 years.
